title: Attacked and defended squares

D0.outcome: Explains that a piece attacks the squares it could capture on, which is not always the set of squares it can move to (pawns capture diagonally; a blocker ends a line).

D1.outcome: Taps every square a named piece attacks in a position with blockers, first with squares lit, then with no aid.

D2.outcome: In mixed positions with no aid, says whether a named square is attacked by White, by Black, by both or by neither, and names the attacking pieces; also marks which of a side's pieces are attacked.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the set of attacked squares changes after a given move (a line opens or closes, a pawn captures, a king steps), including squares newly attacked behind the moved piece.

misconceptions: A pawn attacks the square straight ahead of it.
A piece attacks only squares it could legally move to (so a pinned piece or a pawn's capture squares seem not to count).
A defended piece is not attacked.
conditions: A line piece attacks along its ray only up to and including the first piece in the way; the square behind a blocker is not attacked until the blocker leaves.
A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally ahead, which are different from the squares it moves to.
A pinned piece still attacks its squares for the purpose of what the enemy king may not step on.
contrasts: The pawn's move squares are mistaken for its attack squares (pawn blocked ahead, yet it still attacks two diagonal squares).
A king 'safe' square that a pinned enemy piece still attacks is illegal for the king.
A piece that attacks a square but is itself behind a blocker of the same colour makes no difference to what is attacked now.
